newsitem.title: UK: London Underground skirmish key in election battle.
newsitem.headline: London Underground skirmish key in election battle.

text.p: The fate of the London Underground rail system has become a key issue in the election battle for the capital's voters, with the first skirmish seen this week as Labour and the Conservatives both pledged change if they won.
The fate of world's oldest underground system, known in London as "the Tube", is one policy issue where the ruling Conservatives and the opposition Labour Party differ sharply.
At stake is a network which carries 2.7 million passengers a day, mostly Londoners who will vote on some of the crucial marginal seats that will determine who wins the election.

Prime minister John Major's Conservatives have pledged to privatise the network and re-invest the proceeds in revitalising the system which dates back to the era of Queen Victoria. The price tag could be anywhere between 600 million pounds and 1.5 billion pounds ($983.9 million and $2.5 billion), analysts say.

The Conservatives are looking at three options: privatisation of the entire network as a single entity, splitting the network into franchises for sale or a similar approach to the sale of the national rail network -- with infrastructure sold separately from passenger services.

But Labour, widely tipped to win the May 1 election, says it will keep the metro in public hands and revitalise it through a "private-public partnership", although what this means exactly is yet to be explained.

Andrew Smith, Labour's shadow transport minister, told Reuters his party's plans would be more than diguised private finance initiative (PFI) projects -- the sort of schemes promoted by the current government to help fund new hospitals.
Labour's manifesto said a sale would be a poor deal for taxpayers and passengers, adding "much needed investment would be delayed".
"The core responsibilities of the Underground would be threatened," the Labour manifesto said.
A new opinion poll of London voters, released by capital's Evening Standard newspaper on Friday, claimed Londoners are in the Labour camp on the issue.
Its front page headline screamed "London rejects tube sell-off" with two out of three voters against privatisation.
London Underground's chairman has been in talks with both political camps in recent months, but says it has ideas of its own on the best way forward.
Peter Ford said in an interview he had submitted the metro's latest five-year plan to the government a few days ago.
In it, Ford said if the system received a guaranteed sum of 400-500 million pounds a year for basic running costs it could plan ahead and break even within five years.

"We could wean ourselves off public finances gradually. This is our preferred option. It would require quite a steep rise in productivity, some outsourcing of activities and reduction of staff numbers," said Ford.

He claims the track record for a turnaround is there. Five years ago, the network ran at a seventy million pound loss and is now at a 200 million surplus but that is before the huge cost of maintaining and rebuilding the crumbling system.
"If we were a listed company like ICI (Plc) our share price would have rocketed," said the chairman.
Ford claims both political solutions are flawed. Privatisation will take too long and could lead to continued deterioration in the intervening period leading to a lower sale price.
Labour's plans sounded like PFI, he said, which amounted to buying up investment or service packages from the private sector on a long-term leasing basis.

Public funding for the tube is due to fall to 150 million pounds by 2000. Ford and analysts like Stephen Glaister of the London School of Economics say the Tube needs around 350 million a year just to stand still.
Glaister was sceptical of both party's plans, bearing in mind the major investment needed and the poor state of the system.

"The financial reality is the Underground is a liability not an asset. People have to know how it will be funded in future and neither party has spelled out exactly how they will do that," said Glaister. ($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
